# Transcaval Access for Structural Heart Interventions: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) has become an established treatment for symptomatic severe aortic stenosis across the surgical-risk spectrum. The transfemoral route remains the preferred access, having consistently demonstrated lower morbidity and faster recovery than transthoracic alternatives. However, a meaningful minority of patients have iliofemoral arteries that are too small, tortuous, or calcified to accommodate the large introducer sheaths required for transcatheter heart valves. Caval-aortic access refers to percutaneous entry into the abdominal aorta from the femoral vein through the adjoining inferior vena cava; TAVR is attractive in high-risk or inoperable patients with severe aortic stenosis, but available transcatheter valves require large introducer sheaths, which risk major vascular complications or preclude TAVR altogether [1]. For such patients, transcaval access provides a fully percutaneous alternative that avoids the chest entirely.

## Concept and Preclinical Foundations

The rationale for transcaval access is counterintuitive but physiologically sound. Higher pressure in the relatively confined retroperitoneal space exceeds venous pressure, causing aortic blood to return to the venous circulation through a nearby hole in the inferior vena cava, resulting in an aortocaval fistula rather than hemodynamic collapse [2]. This principle was established in animal models, in which large therapeutic devices could be introduced into the aorta via the inferior vena cava in a simple catheter procedure, and the fistula closed uneventfully despite full anticoagulation, while intentional failure to close the tract was well tolerated and easily redressed [3]. The crossing is performed using transcatheter electrosurgery: from the femoral vein, an electrified guidewire is directed from the inferior vena cava into a snare prepositioned in the adjoining abdominal aorta [4]. The biophysical principles underlying this electrosurgical traversal have since been reviewed in detail [5,6].

## Initial Human Experience and Prospective Validation

The first-in-human series demonstrated proof of concept. Caval-aortic access and tract closure were successful in all 19 patients and TAVR was successful in 17; six patients experienced modified VARC-2 major vascular complications, two of whom required intervention [7]. Notably, the cohort was predominantly female, reflecting the smaller iliofemoral caliber in women [7]. These findings were confirmed in a multicenter prospective investigation, in which transcaval access and closure were successful in 99% of 100 consecutive patients, with no procedural mortality or need for urgent vascular surgery [8]. One-year follow-up further characterized the durability and safety of the technique using off-label nitinol cardiac occluders for closure [9]. Across these experiences, residual aorto-caval fistulae were common at the end of the procedure but the majority closed spontaneously over time [7,8].

## Procedural Planning and Technique

Success depends heavily on patient selection and computed tomographic (CT) planning. Candidates need a calcium-free window on the caval side of the aorta, away from important arterial branches, with no interposed viscera, within reach of an available TAVR introducer sheath; caval-aortic distance does not matter, and most patients ineligible for standard transfemoral access are eligible for transcaval access [10]. Dedicated methods for planning the crossing target and closure on contrast-enhanced CT have been described [11,12], and a detailed how-to guide standardized the access and closure workflow [13]. Standardized endpoint definitions facilitate reporting of outcomes [14]. The technique has been adapted to multiple valve platforms, including the first European transcaval case using an expandable sheath and a SAPIEN 3 valve [15], and the mechanically expandable LOTUS Edge system, where transcaval TAVR was found to be safe and feasible in patients otherwise unsuitable for transfemoral access [16]. Even traversal of synthetic grafts has been reported [17], and laser-assisted crossing offers an alternative energy source [18].

## Comparative Outcomes

Comparative data support transcaval access as a leading non-femoral strategy. In a propensity-weighted analysis drawing on STS/ACC TVT Registry data, transcaval access was used in 238 procedures and transaxillary access in 106, with transfemoral access used in 7,132 procedures [19]. Stroke and transient ischemic attack were 5-fold less common after transcaval than transaxillary access (2.5% vs 13.2%) [19]. Single-center comparative series have reported broadly concordant findings [20]. The initial European multicentre registry confirmed that transfemoral transcaval access proved to be a feasible and safe TAVI approach for high-risk patients with severe aortic stenosis not suitable for transfemoral access [21]. Best-practice consensus documents now codify access and closure techniques and acknowledge that dissemination has been hampered by the historical unavailability of commercially marketed dedicated devices [22].

## Closure Devices and Evolving Technology

A key limitation of early practice was reliance on off-label nitinol cardiac occluders. Transcaval access enables delivery of large-caliber devices to the aorta in patients ineligible for transfemoral arterial access, but persistent aorto-caval fistulae at exit from the catheterization laboratory and bleeding complications were common with off-label occluders [23]. To address this, a dedicated transcaval closure device progressed from concept to first-in-human testing, simplifying large-bore aortic access [23]. Refinements in CT-based selection and in closure technology continue to reduce complications [11,24].

## Beyond TAVR

Transcaval access has broadened beyond aortic valve delivery. Transcaval aortic access has been used for deployment of transcatheter aortic valves where conventional arterial approaches are not feasible, and has been applied to thoracic endovascular aortic repair [25,26]. It has also enabled rapid percutaneous high-flow mechanical circulatory support: vascular access for implantation of mechanical circulatory support in cardiogenic shock is often challenging due to peripheral arterial disease, and transcaval delivery may be an alternative [27,28]. These applications underscore the versatility of the platform for any large-bore aortic intervention [29].

## Conclusion

Transcaval access has matured from an audacious concept into a validated, fully percutaneous strategy for delivering large-bore devices to the aorta when femoral access is unavailable. Supported by preclinical work, prospective registries, and comparative analyses showing favorable neurologic outcomes versus transaxillary access, it now occupies an important place among alternative-access options [30]. The advent of dedicated closure devices and refined CT planning should further improve safety and broaden adoption.
